results.title: NIH Grant Will Fund Autism Research Replication, Validation, and Reproducibility Center | Newsroom | Weill Cornell Medicine
results.content: # NIH Grant Will Fund Autism Research Replication, Validation, and Reproducibility Center. Investigators at Weill Cornell Medicine and Cornell’s Ithaca campus have received a $5.1 million, three-year grant from the National Institutes of Health’s Autism Data Science Initiative (ADSI) to launch the Autism Replication, Validation, and Reproducibility (AR²) Center. “The AR² Center will serve as a scientific quality control hub for the ADSI teams and projects,” said the principal investigator, Dr. Judy Zhong, chief of the Division of Biostatistics in the Department of Population Health Sciences and director of the Data Coordinating Center at Weill Cornell Medicine. The project will be led by Dr. Zhong; Dr. Rainu Kaushal, senior associate dean of health data science at Weill Cornell Medicine and chair of the Department of Population Health Sciences at Weill Cornell Medicine and NewYork-Presbyterian/Weill Cornell Medical Center; and Dr. Conor Liston, professor of neuroscience and psychiatry at Weill Cornell Medicine. AR² will use existing data from previous research, Medicaid claims and other data repositories, including the INSIGHT Clinical Research Network, led by Dr. Kaushal, and PCORnet, to support its analysis of the validity and generalizability of ADSI results. Dr. Zhong and her colleagues will use a three-step process that starts with replicating the data analysis to confirm the initial results reported by ADSI investigators. “We hope to build and ensure trust in ADSI’s research,” Dr. Zhong said. The AR² Center will leverage the advanced computing infrastructure and replication expertise of the Cornell Center for Social Sciences (CCSS) Data and Reproduction Archive at Cornell’s Ithaca campus. The CCSS will help replicate ADSI project results, facilitate data sharing among investigators, collaboratively establish best practices for ADSI projects and host training workshops for ADSI teams, according to co-investigator Dr. Peter Enns, the Robert S. Dr. Zhong said she hopes the three-year project will be just the start of the team’s work improving reproducibility in science more broadly. “We believe it is our responsibility to build on our experience and expertise to enhance trust in scientific research in general,” Dr. Zhong said. Yuri Silvestre-Barbosa1 , Vitória Tavares Castro1 , Larissa Di Carvalho Melo1 , Paula Elaine Diniz Reis2 , André Ferreira Leite1 , Elaine Barros Ferreira2 , Eliete Neves Silva Guerra3. * 1 University of Brasilia, Laboratory of Oral Histopathology, School of Health Sciences, Brasília, Brazil. * 2 University of Brasilia, Interdisciplinary Laboratory of Research applied to Clinical Practice in Oncology, Nursing Department, School of Health Sciences, Brasília, Brazil. * 3 University of Brasilia, Laboratory of Oral Histopathology, School of Health Sciences, Brasília, Brazil. # Worldwide research trends on artificial intelligence in head and neck cancer: a bibliometric analysis. * 1 University of Brasilia, Laboratory of Oral Histopathology, School of Health Sciences, Brasília, Brazil. * 2 University of Brasilia, Interdisciplinary Laboratory of Research applied to Clinical Practice in Oncology, Nursing Department, School of Health Sciences, Brasília, Brazil. * 3 University of Brasilia, Laboratory of Oral Histopathology, School of Health Sciences, Brasília, Brazil. **Objective:** This bibliometric analysis aims to explore scientific data on Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Head and Neck Cancer (HNC). **Study design:** AI-related HNC articles from the Web of Science Core Collection were searched. This analysis covered key characteristics such as sources, authors, affiliations, countries, citations and top cited articles, keyword analysis, and trending topics. The keywords of strong citation revealed 2 main clusters: radiomics and radiotherapy. The most frequently keywords include machine learning, deep learning, artificial intelligence, and head and neck cancer, with recent emphasis on diagnosis, survival prediction, and histopathology. **Conclusions:** There has been an increase in the use of AI in HNC research since 2016 and indicated a notable disparity in publication quantity between high-income and low/middle-income countries. Future research should prioritize clinical validation and standardization to facilitate the integration of AI in HNC management, particularly in underrepresented regions.
